> # Diamond Relaunch! 💎
>
> Diamond is back. We are opening up Diamond submissions again, and now with a new automated preflight check that runs before any version goes to reviewers: Diamond Checks.
>
> Diamond checks surfaces **structural issues** with your submission (broken solution patch or test setup, ambiguous spec, etc.). This is to help you identify issues with your submission before it reaches the QA step. This helps solves the issue of many of y'all starting the QA, realising something is broken, and then having to edit your submission and invalidating all your QA work.
>
> This check takes 30mins-1hr, and we would recommend you **ensure your submission is sound and clean** from obvious defects before committing to it. It will cost 50 tokens per full run. Each step in the run pipeline can be run as well for a specific number of tokens:
>
> - Rollouts - 45 tokens per rollout job (there are 3 rollouts per job)
> - Code Validation - 15 tokens
> - Full Environment QA - 20 tokens
>
> Hinted submissions need to run this pipeline twice, once for unhinted versions and once for hinted versions. Think of this as another form of agent runs but with more evaluation and checks baked in.
>
> There will also be some big changes to the review flow. We are getting rid of reviewer green light where a reviewer gives you the go-ahead to start QA, __**and will instead be using the Diamond Auto Review to give the green light to start QA**__. We will also be doing away with the individual discord channels, and instead, all feedback will be through Shipd. This is generally how a submission cycle will go - only proceed to the next step after addressing everything in the previous step:
>
> 1. Prechecks + Postchecks
> 2. We recommend you run 1x Castor (or even 1x Vega) first to make sure your submission is safe from environment blockers or other obvious defects before doing the full run. Then, run Diamond Checks. If at this point you are confident about your submission then you can also run 10x Castor
> 3. At this point, you will know if you need a hint based on the Castor passrate
> 4. If you Castor passrate = 0%, you will need to add a hint and then run 10x more Castor (hinted). You will then also need to run Diamond Checks again with the hint
> 5. If your Castor passrate is non-zero, you can proceed to the next step.
>    - Run Holistic AI Review as a sanity check
>    - Run Auto Review. If Auto Review approves your submission, you will see a badge on your submission telling you that it is approved for QA. At this point, you can start adding your QA artifacts.
> 6. Once you are done with your QA, you can iterate within the QA loop using the Final QA Review. Your checks will not stale when you iterate on just your QA artifacts (see below on staleness of checks).
> 7. Submit your submission once you are done with the QA. @vibrance will then pick them up and do a review on your submission. They will go through each check and also review your QA artifacts as a final pass. From here the process is similar to normal submissions
> 8. When the reviewer approves, a team member will do one last run-through to finalize it
> 9. Accepted! 🚀
>
> Finally, the difficulty bar has been increased. For diamond submissions, the Castor passrate has to be at most 30%. Aim to create difficult but fair problems.
>
> We are also temporarily throttling Castor runs to cost 25 tokens per run so you can focus on the new Diamond Checks. @catharsis
>
> ## Notes on staleness
>
> Importantly, at each step, your checks will become stale if edits are made and you will need to run them again.
>
> Diamond checks only stale if the following changes:
>
> - description
> - test patch
> - solution patch
> - dockerfile
> - github repo / commit hash
>
> For hinted runs, modifying the hint will only stale the hinted Diamond Checks (similar to hinted Castor runs).
>
> Your QA artifacts will become stale if any edits were made, as long as Castor runs were staled. So we recommend you really examine all the insights from checks made prior (Castor evals, Diamond Checks, the auto review and holistic review) and ensure your submission is as air tight as possible to prevent invalidation of your work. Its much more expensive on your time if issues are remedied later rather than earlier.
>
> However, it is worth noting that once you reach the QA step, you can iterate on your QA artifacts safely with the Final QA Review without worry of staling the other checks, which is why it is important to remedy any issues before this step.
>
> ## Bonuses
>

>
> You will be locked into the Diamond tier for as long as you are part of this programme, and will enjoy increased token drips and cap way above normal Shipd users.
>
> You will also earn $500 USD PER accepted diamond submission and potentially even MORE bonuses for good work.
>
> Happy coding! 🚀 @catharsis @vibrance

> [!IMPORTANT]
> @here 
> Just something I've been noticing lately that might help save your time, efforts and most important, your tokens.
>
> been noticing that some users keep running many agents or adding more hints and clarifications, either in the hints section or indirectly inside the prompt, without first checking why the agents failed or whether the tests are fair.
>
> In many cases, the issue is that the task itself is ambiguous, unfair, or relies on guessing between multiple reasonable approaches because the prompt does not clearly define one, while the tests only accept a specific implementation. We always encourage tests to check the behavioral requirements regardless of the approach the agent takes. But if a specific approach is truly needed, and the tests expect it while other approaches would fail, the prompt must be clear about that.
>
> Please analyze the failures before starting doing the QA or submitting instead of trying to brute force the agents and checks until they pass. It will save you time, tokens, and effort, and it will also improve submission quality and increase the chance of getting approved from the first try.
>
> A good approach is to run a small batch of agents first, then check why they passed or failed. Be honest and realistic with yourself: are the tests truly fair based on the prompt and repo conventions that can be discovered, or are they testing a hidden implementation detail or even contradicting the repo conventions?
>
> A strong signal that there might be an issue is when all or most agents fail for the same exact reason. That could mean there is ambiguity or unfairness in the task, though sometimes it may just mean the task has a genuinely hard part (which is a good thing if it's really fair). Either way, analyze the failures first before moving into full QA so the submission does not get reverted later.

---

Diamond-tier tasks are higher quality tasks with additional requirements:

* Must use **Castor runs**. Requires 10+ runs with 1-3 successes.  
* Requires failure QA:  
  * This is to ensure that tests are fair.  
  * If you find that the tests are unfair or underspecified for any reason in this process, **you need to fix it and re-run the pipeline**.

You can submit new diamond-tier tasks or convert tasks in draft or review into diamond-tier for a higher payout.

## Castor Runs

Unlike normal task submissions, only Castor runs are considered, which cost 10x more. We’ve given you extra tokens for this reason.

## Success Solution Explanation

Submit a high-level summary of the expected solution. Explain it at a high-level that a non-expert of the repo can understand. This will be used as context for understanding the solution.patch.

## Test Summary

For all the f2p (fail to pass) tests, group them into test groups. For each test group, explain what this test group tests and where in the description this requirement is mentioned. Quote parts of the task description for this summary. At the end, ensure that every requirement in the prompt is tested by at least one test group.

## Success Trajectory Analysis

Explain why the implementation is correct, why it meets all the requirements of the description, and does not cause regressions on existing behavior.

Then, if the implementation passes all tests but is not correct, and it is impossible to test this deterministically, provide a detailed explanation of the failure and why it is impossible to test this. For each issue, provide a severity score from 1-5 (4+ is blocking, 3 is borderline, 1-2 is non-blocking) and categorize it as one of correctness, design, extensibility, readability and instruction following.

## Failure QA Instructions 

The goal of Olympus failure analysis is to assess submissions for **fairness**. If the agent fails a test, that failure should reflect a genuine mistake by the agent, not an ambiguous or underspecified task description. The agent should be able to infer the correct behavior from the prompt and codebase alone.

If you find in this process that a task is unfair or suboptimal for any reason, you need to **fix the prompt or verifier and re-run the pipeline**.

For **every test failure** on **every agent run**:

1. **Unfairness check:** Validate that the failure was due to genuine suboptimal agent behaviour instead of ambiguous requirements. Would a seasoned engineer in this codebase not have made this same error? You should: explicitly cite snippets from the prompt, explain how the test case code *correctly* validates the requirement, and if necessary, cite conventions from the codebase to explain any inferred requirements/nuance that the test case assumes.  
2. **Root cause analysis:** Pinpoint to exactly where in the trajectory this error is made and the type of error made. Did the agent make an incorrect assumption or did the agent miss an inferrable edge case? Cite snippets of the solution.

NOTE: A common failure mode is when requirements in the prompt contradict either 1\) each other or 2\) a strongly established code-based convention, which can lead the agent to choose to follow convention over the prompt. If you notice these, you should try to first fix the prompt/verifier to be aligned with the conventions, or if too difficult, use "hint"s to prompt the behavior being tested.

### Example

![][image1]

Bad Response:

1. **Unfairness check:** This is an explicit requirement from the prompt “Zod formatter schemas require defaulted and linked attributes”.  
2. **Root cause analysis:** The readLink requirement did not make it into Zod formatter optionality, whereas readDefault did.

Good Response:

**Unfairness check:** The test case is fair, since it validates a requirement explicitly specified in the prompt “Zod formatter schemas require defaulted and linked attributes”. While the exact setup in the tests

```
+      label: string()
+        .optional()
+        .readLink<typeof schema>(({ pk }) => pk + '-label')
```

seems a bit contradictory, i.e., requiring a seemingly “optional” field to also be required, it is evident from the repo that the `.optional()` modifier here describes optionality of the field’s value in the database (in other words, optional on write), while the `readLink` modifier obviously applies to reads. `ZodFormatter`, and formatters in general, have the role of parsing objects during read, so this behavior of “optional during write” / “required during read” is conventional and consistent.

**Root cause analysis:** Essentially, the agent handled the \`readDefault\` case properly but not the \`readLink\` case. In src/schema/actions/zodSchemer/formatter/utils.ts, the agent extended withOptional to check schema.props.readDefault and, when it's a static value, return zodSchema.default(readDefault) (this also happens to be incorrect logic, since thunk values should also be handled the same). However, it never added a check for schema.props.readLink, so when only readLink is present, the schema gets wrapped in z.optional(), i.e., does not become a required field.

**Environment Description**
Describe what this environment is meant to teach and how the task is set up. Explain what this environment is meant to teach the model and what the task asks for. Use 2-3 sentences, up to a paragraph; link to a doc if more detail is needed.

- We're looking for 300 characters minimum, ideal length is a paragraph (you can attach a link to a document if further details are needed to elaborate).

- Include details about what the environment is meant to teach the model, what a typical task looks like, and how the tasks are set up.

> [!NOTE]
> Example Placeholder :
> e.g. A FastAPI + Postgres inventory service with a race on stock reservation. The task: fix it so concurrent reservations can't oversell, guided by a failing pytest. A successful trajectory makes that test green with a fix scoped to that endpoint. A failing one looks almost right — most tests pass — but trips on one thing: wraps the wrong call in the transaction, or adds an over-broad lock breaking unrelated tests. Teaches scoping concurrency fixes narrowly.

**Placeholders for agent pass/fail analysis**
- Pass:
Explain why this implementation is correct — would it pass a thorough code review by a repo expert? Confirm the task requirements are met, no regressions, no bugs introduced.

If tests pass but the implementation has a real issue (and it's impossible to write a test to catch it), add it below with severity + category.

- Fail:
1. Why are these tests grouped together? (common root cause)
2. Fairness: Would a seasoned engineer have avoided this error? Is the requirement clear?
3. Root cause: Where in the trajectory did the error originate? Bad assumption, missed edge case, or convention over prompt?
